citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The licensee did not provide treatment for two white lions with serious veterinary care issues. The lions have an impaired
ability to walk, lie down, and get up from a lying down position. Between 4-10-2026 and 5-5-2026 no additional diagnoses
and treatment were provided to the lions.
Medical documentation provided by the facility shows prolonged medical concerns for the two lions that was not
appropriately diagnosed. In addition, medical documentation provided by qualified veterinarians cite prolonged improper
nutritional care and lack of diagnosis as the cause of progressive disease conditions present in the two lions. The facility
communicated with the attending veterinarian on 4-10-2026 as confirmed by APHIS officials during an inspection on 4-13-
2026. However, the facility made no changes in methods of diagnosis or treatment of the ongoing, chronic, severe clinical
symptoms displayed by the two lions between 4-13-2026 and 5-5-2026. When the licensee was asked about what
methods to diagnose and/or treat the lions between 4-13-2026 and 5-5-2026 had taken place, he stated “We did not do
any further testing or diagnosis because we sought help from another facility that planned to do the testing when they
received the lions.” The discussion with the other facility did not take place until 5-4-2026 indicating that the facility did not
seek treatment for the lions while they were in their care.
Failing to provide methods to diagnose and/or treat the two lions during this period of time resulted in continued
progression of the chronic disease conditions for the lions, further decline in the health of the lions, delayed treatment,
and a decreased quality of life that may be irreversible or may result in death.
An AWA-licensed exhibitor is responsible for establishing and maintaining programs of adequate veterinary care. Animal
Welfare regulations require that animals receive adequate veterinary care and that an attending veterinarian has
experience and/or training in the care and management of the species being attended. Each exhibitor shall establish and
maintain programs of adequate veterinary care that include the use of appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose,
and treat diseases and injuries must be provided by the licensee.
To be corrected from this time moving forward.

The public was having contact with the animals and there was not a readily identifiable attendant present in different
areas of the facility to include:
- In the "Big Barn" directly across from the entrance, members of the public were observed petting and feeding two
camels and approximately fifteen cows.
- In the petting zoo area, housing 9 goats, 8 sheep, and 1 audad members of the public were observed in the enclosure
interacting with the animals. An adult and three children were observed trying to enter the enclosure when 4-6 goats
entered the lock-out area between the two gates going into the enclosure with the members of the public. An employee
was called on the radio with a “code billy” announcement and he arrived to let the goats out of the small area freeing the
members of the public allowing them entrance into the enclosure.
- The enclosure housing 2 young camels, members of the public were observed having contact with the animals.
- In the area between the "Big Barn" and the office, the facility has a trail along the enclosures housing 6 camels, 2
alpaca, 1 pig, 3 llamas and 2 emus where the public is encouraged to feed and interact with the animals. Several
members of the public were observed having public contact to include a large group of children.
Allowing public contact without an attendant present can lead to injuries to the animals and/or the public.
The facility needs to have a responsible, knowledgeable, and readily identifiable employee or attendant present at all
times during periods of public contact to ensure the safety of the animals and the members of the public.
To be corrected by June 17, 2026.

Two baby red ruffed lemurs were observed on top of an enclosure housing one brown lemur that was one enclosure over
from their intended enclosure. Their enclosure was located in the “Small Barn” on the end closest to the petting zoo. The
lemurs were two to three weeks old and had just started venturing out on their own and away from their mother according
to the facility representative.
Enclosures that do not contain the animals securely can lead to injury to the baby lemurs by other animals or unsafe
items/conditions outside of their intended enclosure. The enclosure for the baby red ruffed lemurs, and any other baby
nonhuman primates needs to be constructed in a manner to contain them securely to prevent them from escaping and
being injured.
The licensee needs to ensure that all housing facilities for nonhuman primates are kept in good repair, protect the animals
from injury, contain the animals securely, and restrict other animals from entering.
To be corrected by June 17, 2026.

The facility had several areas where the housing facilities were not being maintained in good repair to include:
- The back goat enclosure housing 18 goats had a plastic slide, a plastic castle climbing structure, and a black water tank
that had been flipped upside down to protect an irrigation valve that had areas that were broken and cracked.
The structures in the goat enclosure create a potential for injury if the goats were to climb/jump on them and their feet/legs
were to fall through the cracks.
Housing facilities need to be maintained in good repair to protect the animals from injury.
Corrected prior to the exit briefing.

The facility had an established pest control program however, several areas within the facility were observed to have
signs of insects and mammalian pests indicating that the pest control program is not effective. The areas where this was
observed included the following:
- There were wasps observed on the ceiling of the enclosure housing the porcupine and in the shed provided for the 18
goats in the back goat enclosure. Corrected by the time of the exit briefing.
- In the feed preparation area of the "Small Barn," there were numerous flies observed throughout the area to include on
the packaged meat sitting on the counter, in and near the biscuits for primates, and around the areas storing fruits and
vegetables. There was an open window without a screen and two open trash cans filled with debris that were attracting
flies to the area.
- In the food storage area in the middle of the “Big Barn,” ants were observed behind the bags of feed and there was
evidence of mouse droppings on the shelves, ledges, and on some of the bags of feed.
Pests can transmit disease, contaminate food and surfaces, and can harm animals. The presence of wasps, flies, ants,
and mouse droppings indicates that there is not an established and maintained program to control insects and
mammalian pests. As a result, this can increase the disease hazards, contaminate food and surfaces, and can cause
harm to the animals.
A safe and effective program for the control of insects, ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests needs to be
established and maintained to ensure the health and well-being of the animals throughout the facility.
To be corrected by 6/24/2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
Additional Inspectors:
Ronald Richardson, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
